Eight image generators compared on control, style consistency, commercial rights and cost — plus where each one still ruins a picture.

An image generator is no longer one product category. The same prompt produces a photorealistic scene in one tool, an illustration in a second, and a logo with readable lettering in a third, so choosing by demo reel rather than by job gets expensive fast.

Eight tools below, grouped by what they are actually good at rather than by hype. Each entry says who should use it, how it is usually paid for, and the specific thing it still gets wrong.

How we picked

The criteria were control over style and composition, consistency across a series of images, clarity on commercial rights, and an output publishable without retouching. We skipped generators that offer a handful of renders before the paywall, and we ignored benchmark claims we could not reproduce ourselves in an ordinary browser.

What it means for you: if you make images for clients or products, rights and repeatability matter more than the single prettiest render. A tool whose output you cannot legally use is not a tool.

One warning before the list: every generator below is convincing on its own showcase images. The differences appear on the twentieth image of a series, when style, palette and proportions have to survive from one render to the next without manual repair.

Photography and general image-making

These four solve different problems despite sharing a category. The first two optimise for interpreting a written brief, the third for convenience inside an ecosystem you already use, and the fourth for repetition across a set of images. Choose from the wrong group and even a strong tool will disappoint.

1. Midjourney

Still the strongest aesthetic default: the fastest route to an image that looks like finished art rather than a first draft. It works through a web interface and Discord, which is a genuine friction point if you wanted a plain upload box. Who it is for: concept work, mood boards and cover images where mood beats literal accuracy. Where it fails: precise edits and specific layouts, and its commercial terms are worth reading yourself rather than taking from a list like this one.

2. ChatGPT image generation

Strongest at following instructions in plain language: put this text in the image, keep the character consistent, change only the background. It behaves like a patient designer rather than a randomiser, which makes iteration far less frustrating. Who it is for: explanatory graphics, quick mock-ups and anything containing lettering. Where it fails: photographic realism, and heavy use consumes your allowance quickly on both free and paid plans.

3. Google Gemini image tools

Convenience wins here: generation sits inside an assistant many people already use, with edits and variations handled conversationally. Quality is competitive for everyday and marketing images. Who it is for: people inside the Google ecosystem who want a picture without learning a new interface. Where it fails: fine control and stylistic range — and Google's terms on how prompts and outputs are handled deserve a read if you work with client material.

4. Leonardo AI

A platform of models and presets rather than one look, with control over style, composition and reference images that Midjourney deliberately withholds. A usable free allowance is why it survives on lists like this one. Who it is for: people producing a series who need the same style to repeat across frames. Where it fails: the interface is dense, and model sprawl means results shift more than you expect between settings.

Design, brands and readable text

5. Adobe Firefly

The option to consider when an image has to survive a legal review: Adobe trained Firefly on licensed and public-domain material and positions it for commercial work. Its most useful form is generative fill inside Photoshop and Illustrator, where you repair a picture instead of replacing it. Who it is for: agencies and marketing teams with brand and rights requirements. Where it fails: the free credit allowance is limited, and raw photorealism trails the best rivals.

6. Ideogram

The pick when lettering matters: signs, posters, packaging mock-ups and social posts where one misspelled word ruins the result. It renders type more reliably than most competitors, though you should still proof it at full size. Who it is for: design concepts that contain real words. Where it fails: photographic texture and complex scenes, and any passage of text longer than a word still comes out wrong occasionally.

7. Canva Magic Studio

Not the most capable generator but the most practical one for non-designers: generation happens inside the editor where the rest of the layout already lives, with resizing, background removal and brand kits one click away. Who it is for: social teams, teachers and small businesses producing steady volume. Where it fails: a lower creative ceiling, limited free credits, and premium results that carry a watermark until you pay.

The open-source option

8. Stable Diffusion, self-hosted

The only route with no per-image cost, no vendor content policy and full control over weights, models and extensions. You run it on your own hardware or rent a GPU, which changes the economics entirely at volume. Who it is for: high-volume work, privacy-sensitive prompts and tinkerers who want to tune a pipeline. Where it fails: setup is a project in itself — model files, nodes, settings — and quality depends on work you do yourself.

What they still get wrong

Three recurring problems. Rights remain murky outside licensed tools: copyright treatment of purely machine-generated images varies by country and the underlying litigation is unresolved, so keep records of how an image was made — our AI copyright guide covers the current position. Consistency breaks: character, palette and lighting drift between generations, which is why serious work uses references and editing rather than regeneration. Small details fail: hands, jewellery, repeated patterns and long text need inspection at full size.

What it means for you: build a checking step into the workflow. Open every result at 100 percent, read all lettering, and save the prompt and tool name with the file so you can later show where it came from.

There is also a workflow problem nobody advertises. Most tools are poor at editing one region of an existing image without disturbing the rest, so production work still ends in a raster editor. Generation gets you the material; composition and repair remain manual skills.

Verdict

For quick, controllable iteration, ChatGPT's image generation. For finished-looking art, Midjourney. For commercial work that will be scrutinised, Firefly — and if you generate at volume or need privacy, self-hosted Stable Diffusion is the only economics that make sense. Everything else is a compromise between those four, usually on price or on convenience.

Our Midjourney versus DALL-E comparison goes deeper on the two best-known names, and the free tools roundup lists the generators you can try before paying for anything.

Frequently asked questions

Which AI image generator is best for commercial work?

Adobe Firefly is the safest starting point because Adobe trains it on licensed and public-domain material and markets it for commercial use. Midjourney and several other services also grant commercial rights on paid plans. Whatever you choose, keep the prompt, the tool and the date with the file, and check the terms yourself before the image goes into paid work.

Why does text in AI-generated images keep coming out misspelled?

Image models do not read text the way software does; they predict shapes that look like lettering, so unusual words and long phrases are the first to break. Newer tools handle short labels well, but anything longer than a couple of words should be checked at full size or replaced with real type in a design tool afterwards.

Can I post AI images without saying they are AI?

Platform rules differ, and some require synthetic media to be labelled, especially realistic images of people or events. Even where disclosure is not mandatory, undisclosed AI images carry a reputational risk: audiences react badly to fakes discovered later. For commercial accounts the safer habit is to disclose when asked and keep provenance records for anything that could be questioned.
